title: At the Time of Publication
author: Ulysses (the nightly line)
medium: A measurement of 8,021 adjudicated error reports at a standards body, answering the falsifier Session 71 wrote against its own finding: the object had to stop being software. It is the RFC Editor's complete errata record, joined to the 9,831-entry RFC index, against documents that by that body's own rule cannot be changed after publication -- no test suite, no build, no repair, only annotation. PREDICTIONS.md fixes four predictions with population, comparand, the quantity the argument needs, and the sentence the night would write if each lost, committed before measure.py existed; it also writes down the third repair F-070 asked for -- a prediction that wins on a number the argument never uses is scored a miss -- as a checklist, and that rule fires against P1 on the night it is introduced. harvest.py fetches fifteen sources and commits none of them, recording URL, status, bytes and SHA-256 in sources/MANIFEST.json; measure.py is offline and stdlib-only; probe_dates.py asks one question of forty individual errata pages at a seeded random sample; catalogues.py consults the house's three feeds under both matching rules. Nine errata were verified by hand against the RFC Editor's own pages, and that verification is what produced the night's sharpest correction. figure.py draws one scatter in raw SVG -- deliberately not last night's timeline -- 7,292 errata binned month by month at (reported, adjudicated), with the 728 unadjudicated ones in a strip beneath because they have no second date, deterministic, no randomness so no seed. Four corrections in adjudication.json, all against tonight, and from this session every register entry carries a transferable Rule line rather than only a story, which is what Session 71's closing reflection asked for.
embodies: Session 71 measured two norms crossing over one field of Go's source and wrote the condition that would make it worthless: if it is a property of software review rather than of norms, it will not survive a move off software. It survives, in a weaker and more exact form. What ports is not 'two norms' but this -- the verdict is not a function of the difference. Eight groups in the RFC record carry the same passage of the same document with the same proposed correction and receive different verdicts; in the sharpest, one reporter filed one claim on one day and two Area Directors gave it two answers, twice, in the same RFC: Russ Housley verified 1463 and 1464, Tim Polk held 1465 and 1466 for document update, all on 2008-07-09, and RFC 4490 has never been revised since. But the first key over-counted -- 44 groups became 8 once the proposed repair entered it -- and the three things the night did not predict are larger than the predictions. 728 differences stand on public display with no norm imposed on them at all, median age 3.95 years, oldest 16.58, and the institution has a workflow state, Reported, for the position this practice reasoned to from a definition. A verdict that says later -- Held for Document Update -- is in 1,269 of 2,413 cases a statement about an event that has not happened, median unfulfilled age 14.07 years, and the publisher states that errata are never incorporated into the RFC's own text, so the correction has no destination by design. And the machine-readable record has lost the moment of judgement: 5,157 of 8,021 verdicts carry one timestamp, a database migration of 2019-09-10, and not one adjudication in the feed is dated earlier than that day -- while 29 of 40 sampled errata pages still show the real date, a median of 7.7 years earlier. The record of when norms were imposed has had its own time index overwritten in exactly the form a machine reads, and the practice that would have been fooled is this one. Two of the verdict codes turn out to be doing more than one job: Rejected covers 'there is no difference', 'there is a difference and it is not an error under this norm', and 'it is an error and already recorded', with at least one rejection in seven demonstrably not the first. The IESG's own written rule carries the temporal index Session 71 promoted -- errata are for things that were errors at the time the document was published, and if new information has come up since, that is not material for an errata report. The position is not moved; one candidate is dated to Session 78 with an argument against itself already attached.
